summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement, Priscilla S Redd, Chunwan Lu, Alyssa D Merting, Dakota B Poschel, Dafeng Yang, Gang Zhou, David H Munn, Kebin Liu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the mechanism by which tumor-expressed PD-L1 (tPD-L1) promotes immune suppression, specifically focusing on lung metastasis in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and colorectal cancer (CRC) models. Contrary to the prevailing paradigm that tPD-L1 directly inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activity via PD-1 engagement, the authors demonstrate that tPD-L1 has no direct effect on CTL killing when only tumor cells and CTLs are present. Instead, tPD-L1 functions by engaging PD-1 on myeloid cells (mPD-1), creating an immunosuppressive niche that suppresses type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. Using CRISPR-Cas9 knockout models of 4T1 and CT26 cells, the study shows that while PD-L1 loss does not affect primary tumor growth, it significantly reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1 activates SHP-2, which dephosphorylates STAT1, thereby repressing the expression of chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. This repression impairs the recruitment of CTLs to the lung metastatic site. The study further validates these findings in human patient cohorts, showing that response to PD-1 blockade immunotherapy correlates with the restoration of IFN-I signaling in myeloid cells. The authors conclude that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis is critical for controlling CTL infiltration in lung metastasis, providing a mechanistic basis for the efficacy of checkpoint blockade in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. This work shifts the focus from direct CTL inhibition to myeloid-mediated suppression of chemokine production, highlighting the importance of the tumor microenvironment in metastatic progression.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the mechanism by which tumor-expressed PD-L1 (tPD-L1) promotes immune suppression, specifically focusing on lung metastasis in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and colorectal cancer (CRC) models. Contrary to the prevailing paradigm that tPD-L1 directly inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activity via PD-1 engagement, the authors demonstrate that tPD-L1 has no direct effect on CTL killing when only tumor cells and CTLs are present. Instead, tPD-L1 functions by engaging PD-1 on myeloid cells (mPD-1), creating an immunosuppressive niche that suppresses type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. Using CRISPR-Cas9 knockout models of 4T1 and CT26 cells, the study shows that while PD-L1 loss does not affect primary tumor growth, it significantly reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1 activates SHP-2, which dephosphorylates STAT1, thereby repressing the expression of chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. This repression impairs the recruitment of CTLs to the lung metastatic site. The study further validates these findings in human patient cohorts, showing that response to PD-1 blockade immunotherapy correlates with the restoration of IFN-I signaling in myeloid cells. The authors conclude that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis is critical for controlling CTL infiltration in lung metastasis, providing a mechanistic basis for the efficacy of checkpoint blockade in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. This work shifts the focus from direct CTL inhibition to myeloid-mediated suppression of chemokine production, highlighting the importance of the tumor microenvironment in metastatic progression.

Research Context
The mechanism of tPD-L1 induction of immune suppression via an intermediate cell is incompletely understood. PD-L1 and PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade is believed to function by blocking PD-L1 to PD-1 engagement. Particular attention has been paid to the role of tumor-expressed PD-L1 as a direct molecular shield. Emerging data suggests response to PD-1/L1 blockade may depend on tumor anatomic sites. The dominant cause of mortality is metastatic growth, not primary tumor growth. How tPD-L1 might differentially drive metastasis from primary tumor is unknown. PD-1 expression in non-T cell populations is important for tumor immune evasion. How non-T cell-expressed PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression is incompletely understood.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether tPD-L1 directly protects tumor cells from CTL cytotoxicity. The authors hypothesize that tPD-L1 targets myeloid cell-expressed PD-1 to suppress type I IFN. This suppression represses Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 expression in myeloid cells. This impairs CTL recruitment to the lung niche to enhance established lung metastasis. The study aims to determine if tPD-L1 exhibits no direct effect on CTL activity. It is hypothesized that a third factor in the lung metastatic niche is necessary. The hypothesis is that tPD-L1 engages mPD-1 to antagonize type I interferon signaling. The predicted outcome is that PD-L1 loss will decrease lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner.

Methodological Details
The study used 4T1 murine triple negative breast cancer and CT26 colorectal cancer cell lines. Cd274 encoding PD-L1 was deleted using CRISPR-Cas9 in these cell lines. An in vitro CTL-tumor interaction system using 2/20 tumor-specific CTLs was utilized. 2/20 cells recognize the H2-Ld-restricted AH1 epitope of gp70 protein. In vivo models included orthotopic injection for primary tumors and tail vein injection for metastasis. Lung metastasis was quantified by harvesting lungs and inflating with India ink solution. RNA sequencing was performed on lungs colonized by WT and PD-L1-deficient 4T1 cells. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on CD45+ leukocytes from colonized lungs. Approximately 7500 cells were analyzed using UMAP for dimensional reduction. Flow cytometry was used to validate transcriptomic data in 4T1-colonized lungs. Myeloid cells were depleted using clodronate liposomes in tumor-bearing mice. Human patient data from metastatic basal cell carcinoma was analyzed. Statistical analysis was conducted using Prism8 and two-tailed Student's t-test. Bulk RNA sequencing used STARv2.5 for alignment and DESeq2 for quantification. Single-cell libraries were generated using the Chromium Single Cell 3' Reagent Kit v3.

Procedures And Architectures
HEK293FT cells were co-transfected with pCMV-VSV-G, psPAX2, and lentiCRISPRv2 plasmids. Tumor cells were transduced with lentivirus and selected with puromycin. Cells were sorted for marker-negative cells using a BD FACSARIA. 4T1 orthotopic tumors were established by injection at the right second mammary gland. CT26 subcutaneous tumors were established by injection at the right flank. For experimental metastasis, tumor cells were injected into the lateral tail vein. Anti-CD8α or isotype control antibodies were injected i.v. every other day. Samples were blocked in FACS Buffer containing mouse FcBlock. Intracellular staining was performed using Cytofix/Cytoperm Plus kit. Data was acquired on FACSCalibur or LSRFortessa and analyzed with FlowJo v10.6.0. RNA was extracted using Direct-zol RNA microprep kit. Reads were aligned to mm10 reference genome using STARv2.5. scRNA-seq libraries were sequenced on Illumina NextSeq 500 platform. Cells were clustered using the first fifty principal components. Clusters were annotated by comparison to pre-existing RNA-sequencing datasets using SingleR.

Key Results
tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage when an antigen-specific effector CTL encounters a tumor cell. No difference was observed in primary tumor growth between PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 cells. Knocking out PD-L1 in tumor cells significantly decreases lung metastasis. Increased infiltration of CD3+ cells was observed in the lung after loss of tPD-L1. No difference in initial tumor cell colonization was seen one day after tail vein injection. PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in RAGII-KO mice. Genetic ablation of MHC class I and CD8+ T cell depletion revealed tPD-L1 drives metastasis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed tPD-L1 engages myeloid PD-1 to antagonize type I IFN. Expression changes were observed in myeloid cells, not CTLs, in the metastatic niche. Enhanced antigen presentation machinery was detected in macrophages following tPD-L1 loss. Pdcd1lg2 encoding PD-L2 was identified as a marker for IFN-stimulated myeloid cells. Engagement with 4T1 tPD-L1 enhanced SHP-2 activation and decreased pSTAT1 levels. Disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFNβ production. Depletion of myeloid cells diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting lung tumor growth. Human patient response to PD-1 blockade correlates with IFN-I response in myeloid cells.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study uncouples the role of tPD-L1 at the metastatic site from primary tumor growth. tPD-L1 binds to mPD-1 to enforce an immunologically cold microenvironment. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration. This axis underlies the efficacy of ICB immunotherapy in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. The PD-1/L1 axis functions as a negative feedback circuit for type I interferon. Low response rates in interferon alpha therapies may be due to compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. Type I interferon signaling is essential for myeloid cell function in CTL recruitment. This work highlights the importance of myeloid cells in bridging tPD-L1 to CTL suppression.

Contradictions And Limitations
Conflicting findings for the role of tPD-L1 in PD-1 blockade efficacy have been reported. There is a consensus that tPD-L1 may be sufficient but not necessary for response. One limitation is that the study exclusively analyzed lung metastases. Lung metastases may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment due to barrier tissue location. The mechanism underlying tPD-L1 induction of immune suppression via an intermediate cell is incompletely understood. How non-T cell-expressed PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression is incompletely understood.

Claims
tPD-L1 does not directly suppress CTL activation or lytic function when only tumor cells and CTLs are present. In vitro cytotoxicity results show no difference in killing between WT and KO cells. 2/20 CTLs exert antigen-specific cytotoxicity within minutes. Previous paradigms suggest tPD-L1 serves as a direct molecular shield against CTL lysis. This shifts the focus to indirect mechanisms involving other cell types.
tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis by engaging myeloid PD-1 to suppress type I interferon signaling. PD-L1 loss significantly decreases lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. Single-cell RNA sequencing shows tPD-L1 antagonizes type I IFN in myeloid cells. Depletion of myeloid cells impairs tPD-L1 promotion of lung metastasis. No difference in primary tumor growth was observed. This identifies a new axis for CTL recruitment control in metastasis.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ablation of MHC class I and CD8+ T cells confirmed the CTL-dependent nature of the effect. Depletion of myeloid cells using clodronate liposomes validated the role of myeloid cells. Disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFNβ production. The study used both bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing for robust validation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage in in vitro CTL-tumor interaction. Figure 2 shows no difference in primary tumor growth between WT and KO cells. Figure 3 shows increased CD3+ infiltration in lung after tPD-L1 loss. Figure 4 shows single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ leukocytes from colonized lungs. Figure 5 shows validation of transcriptomic data by flow cytometry. Figure 6 shows tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1 creates an immunosuppressive niche. Figure 7 shows human patient response to PD-1 blockade correlates with IFN-I response.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis in lung metastasis. 2. The strongest evidence is the significant decrease in lung metastasis upon PD-L1 knockout in a CTL-dependent manner. 3. The future path involves exploring this axis in other metastatic sites and clinical trials.
